slides.headline: He could have run. He chose the poison.
slides.sub: Jacques-Louis David, The Death of Socrates, 1787

slides.headline: Athens, 399 BC
slides.text: Athens condemns its wisest man. Socrates, about 70, is accused of corrupting the young. His sentence: drink a cup of hemlock.

slides.headline: Still teaching
slides.text: His friends had arranged an escape. He refused it. Now, in his last minutes, he is still teaching, one hand raised toward the sky.

slides.headline: The cup
slides.text: His other hand reaches for the poison without even looking at it. Yet the young man handing it over cannot bear to watch.

slides.headline: Crito
slides.text: His old friend Crito grips his leg, pleading with his eyes. And under Crito, David signed his full name.

slides.headline: The old man
slides.text: At the foot of the bed, an old man slumps, turned away from it all. This is Plato, who later wrote the scene down.

slides.headline: A deliberate mistake
slides.text: But Plato was young then, and he wasn't even in the room. David made him old, and painted his own initials under him.

slides.headline: Leaving
slides.text: Up the stairs, his wife Xanthippe turns back for one last look, as she is led away.

slides.headline: His choice
slides.text: Paris called it a masterpiece in 1787. Socrates chose death over running from his own beliefs. Would you have taken the escape?
